message.content: Lions (family Felidae) and zebras (family Equidae) belong to very different orders—Carnivora and Perissodactyla, respectively. Their most recent common ancestor is therefore a member of the clade that contains all placental mammals (Eutheria). This ancestor would have been a small, shrew‑like mammal that lived during the Paleocene epoch, roughly 70–80 million years ago.
message.reasoning:
The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want the common ancestor of lion and zebra. This is a biology question. The common ancestor would be the last common ancestor of the family Felidae (lion) and Equidae (zebra). That would be a mammal from the order Carnivora for lion and order Perissodactyla for zebra. The last common ancestor of all mammals? Actually, lion and zebra diverged at the level of the clade that includes all placental mammals. But maybe they want the last common ancestor of the two species: the last common ancestor of lions and zebras would be an ancestor of all placental mammals, which is a mammal from the group Eutheria. But if we want a more specific answer: the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae would be a member of the clade that includes all placental mammals, specifically the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be a mammal from the clade that includes all placental mammals, likely a small mammal from the Paleocene epoch.

But perhaps the user expects something like "the last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, shrew-like mammal that lived around 70 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a mammal from the clade that includes all placental mammals."

Alternatively, the user might want the last common ancestor of the two species: the last common ancestor of lions and zebras is a mammal from the clade that includes all placental mammals, which existed about 100 million years ago. But we can give a more precise answer: the last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, insectivorous mammal that lived during the Paleocene epoch, around 65-70 million years ago.

We can also mention that the last common ancestor of the two species belongs to the clade that includes all placental mammals, specifically the clade that includes the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla. So the last common ancestor would have been a small, possibly insectivorous mammal that lived around 70 million years ago.

Thus, the answer: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a small, shrew-like mammal that lived around 70 million years ago, belonging to the clade of placental mammals. Alternatively, we could say "the last common ancestor of lions and zebras was a mammal from the clade that includes all placental mammals, likely a small, insectivorous mammal from the Paleocene epoch."
